definitions.definition: For each nonnegative integer k, Eucl(k)=R^k is the space of real k-tuples, with distance (sum_{j=1}^k |x_j-y_j|^2)^(1/2) and its Borel sigma algebra. The empty tuple is the sole point of Eucl(0). Eucl(k)×R is identified with Eucl(k+1) by adjoining the last coordinate; this identification uses the Euclidean distance sqrt(||x-y||_2^2+|t-u|^2).

definitions.type: diameter function on subsets of metric or extended metric spaces
definitions.definition: diam(A)=sup{dist(x,y): x,y in A}, as an extended nonnegative number, with supremum of the empty set zero. Thus diam(empty)=0. In ordinary Euclidean spaces a nonempty set of diameter zero is a singleton. Native ediam is this extended-valued diameter. Euclidean finite diameters are identified with their nonnegative real values.

binders.type: subset of a metric or extended metric space

definitions.type: positive exponent and scale Hausdorff contents and limiting Hausdorff measure on Euclidean sets
definitions.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero.

binders.type: countable family of subsets of the same Euclidean space

definitions.type: real exponent → Borel Hausdorff measure on any extended metric space
definitions.definition: muH(a) denotes the native unnormalized Borel Hausdorff measure MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure a. It is obtained by the metric outer-measure construction mkMetric with gauge r↦r^a on extended nonnegative diameters: at each positive scale take the maximal outer measure bounded by the gauge on all nonempty sets of at most that diameter, then take the supremum over scales and its Borel-measure realization. Values on arbitrary sets mean outer-measure values. Empty covering members cost zero and nonempty members cost diam^a with extended nonnegative-real powers; at a=0 a nonempty singleton has cost 1.

definitions.type: Hausdorff dimension of subsets of metric spaces, valued in [0,infinity]
definitions.definition: dimH(A), also written dim_H A, is the standard Hausdorff dimension: sup({a≥0 : muH(a)(A)=infinity}) in [0,infinity], where the supremum of an empty set is 0. This is the native dimH definition. The notation uses the empty-set dimension convention 0. Critical-exponent properties and agreement with the supplied positive-exponent diameter-cost measure are proof obligations, not extra assumptions.

binders.type: subset of an extended metric space

definitions.definition: D=dimH(E), initially an extended nonnegative real. Real arithmetic involving D is used only after its finiteness is proved.

inputs.statement: E is compact in the Euclidean metric of R^n.

For every nonnegative integer k, every A⊆Eucl(k), and every real a>0, H^a(A)=muH(a)(A). Consequently: a>dimH(A) implies H^a(A)=0; 0<a<dimH(A) implies H^a(A)=infinity; H^a(A)=0 implies dimH(A)≤a; and H^a(A)=infinity implies dimH(A)≥a. Hausdorff dimension is nonnegative. For A⊆B⊆Eucl(k), dimH(A)≤dimH(B). For every nonnegative integer l and every distance-preserving map g:A→Eucl(l), dimH(g(A))=dimH(A).

output.statement: 0≤D≤n, so D is finite. Also, for every s>0 and delta>0, H^s_delta(E)<infinity.

locals.declaration: Choose L>0 with E⊆[-L,L]^n, whose existence was proved in F001.
Consider arbitrary positive exponents s; in S002 first impose s>n, then in S003-S004 use any s>0.
Fix an arbitrary delta>0, used for the grid-cover scale in S002 and for the finite-content assertion in S004.

argument.text: H003 says E is compact. Compact subsets of Euclidean space are bounded: the open balls centered at the origin with positive integer radii cover the space, so a finite subcover of E puts it inside one such ball. Hence there exists a real L>0 with E⊆[-L,L]^n. Record this existence before choosing L.

produces.statement: There exists L0>0 such that E⊆[-L0,L0]^n.

argument.text: Choose L as in F001 and set C=(2L+2)^n. By H001, n≥0; first take the branch L1: n≥1. For 0<h≤1, divide each coordinate interval [-L,L] into at most ceil(2L/h) closed intervals of length at most h. The resulting grid contains at most (2L/h+1)^n≤C h^(-n) cubes, each of diameter at most sqrt(n) h, and covers E. For any s>n the total s-cost is at most C n^(s/2) h^(s-n), which tends to zero as h decreases to zero. At each fixed target scale take h≤delta/sqrt(n) and then h arbitrarily small; H^s_delta(E)=0 at every scale, hence H^s(E)=0. N001 yields D≤s for every s>n, so D≤n. N001 also gives 0≤D. This proves the branch L1 implication; discharge L1.

For the other branch L2: n=0, H002 and the single empty tuple give E=Eucl(0), a singleton. A singleton cover has diameter 0 and zero s-cost for every s>0, so H^s(E)=0 for all s>0. N001 gives D≤s for every s>0, and D≥0, hence D=0. Discharge L2. Since the nonnegative integer n is either zero or at least one, the two branches and F002 give 0≤D≤n, in particular finite D.

Finally let s>0 and delta>0. The family of open balls centered at points of E with radius delta/4 covers E. By H003 it has a finite subcover. Each such ball has diameter at most delta/2≤delta, and its s-cost is finite; for n=0 its diameter is 0. Thus this finite admissible cover has finite total cost, so H^s_delta(E)<infinity. Together with F003 this is the exported claim.
